opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, honestly. A while back I was pretty skeptical. If a big training run broke, the last thing I wanted was some model poking around in the infra code. These jobs are expensive, the failure modes are subtle, and debugging them depends so much on context: sharding configs, weird hardware issues, some flag someone set three months ago. I didn't think a coding assistant could reason about any of that.

What changed is that I started using these tools on smaller things first, like stack traces, config mismatches, and "why is this loss spiking" kinds of investigations. They got surprisingly good at it. Often they'd find the issue faster than I would, mainly because they read through all the logs and the code without getting tired or making assumptions. At some point I noticed I was just pasting the error in and letting it go, and it would come back with a fix that was actually correct.

So now my default is much closer to trusting it to take a first pass. I'll let it diagnose, propose a fix, sometimes even apply it and relaunch. I still review anything that touches the core model code or anything that could silently corrupt a run, because the scary bugs are the ones that don't crash, they just make your model slightly worse. But the overall shift is real. It went from "I'd never let it near my training job" to "why would I debug this myself first?" That's been a pretty big mindset change for me, and I think for a lot of researchers.

r001.rationale: The speaker says the tools often find training-job issues faster than they do and can return a correct fix, conveying that the model may know how to fix the job better.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's flipped almost completely, and I think the interesting part is how it flipped.

A couple of years ago, when I was at Google and then early on with Reka, my instinct was that the training stack was the one place I would never let an agent touch. Training jobs are this weird category of bug. You get a loss spike at step forty thousand, or your throughput drops twenty percent after a checkpoint restore, and the cause could be a data shard, a numerical thing in attention, some TPU topology quirk, a stale compile cache. The feedback loop is hours, sometimes a day. So the cost of a wrong fix is not "the test fails," it's "you burned a day of a very expensive cluster." That made me extremely conservative. I would use the tools for scaffolding, for writing eval harnesses, for the boring glue, but when the actual run was sick, I was in there myself.

What changed is two things. One, the models got genuinely better at the kind of reasoning that debugging a run needs, which is not really coding, it's more like differential diagnosis. The good ones now will say, look, your gradient norm is fine, your loss spiked only on this subset of steps, go check whether those steps correspond to a particular data mixture boundary. That's the question I would have asked. Two, and this is the bigger one, I changed how I set things up around the tool. I stopped asking it to fix the job and started asking it to tell me what it would do and why, and I give it very cheap ways to verify. Run the step on a tiny slice, replay the exact batch that spiked, diff the config against the last known good run. When the agent can actually check its hypothesis for a few cents instead of a few thousand dollars, I'm happy to let it go pretty far on its own.

So I'd say my trust didn't go up because I decided to be braver. It went up because I made the blast radius smaller. I still don't let anything restart a large run unsupervised. But the diagnosis, the first few hypotheses, the patch to the data loader, the "go check if this is the same bug we hit in March" — that's increasingly something I'll kick off from my phone and look at later.

The thing I'm still a bit skeptical of is the confident wrong answer. These systems are very good at producing a plausible story for a loss spike, and a plausible story is dangerous in ML because so many things are confounded. So the trust is real, but it's trust with receipts. If it can't show me the experiment that supports the fix, I treat it like a smart intern who just read the codebase, which is still enormously useful, but it's not the person who gets to press the button yet.

r001.rationale: The response says newer models can reason well about debugging and gives an example of a question the speaker would also have asked. It does not express that a model might know better than the speaker how to fix a training job.

astra-6.text: I’ve become a lot more willing to let them try. With a training job, though, there’s a difference between fixing the error and fixing the underlying problem. You can make the code run and still be training the wrong thing. So I’m happy to delegate more of the debugging, but I still want to understand the change and check what the training is actually doing. The trust comes from seeing those fixes hold up, rather than just seeing the exception disappear.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker is more willing to delegate debugging, but it does not express that an AI coding model might know better than the speaker how to fix the job.

sol-6.1.text: I think the bar is different for writing code and fixing a training job. I’m happy to let a coding tool propose a fix, but I still want to understand what it changed. A job crashing is obvious; a job that runs but quietly trains the wrong thing is much harder to catch. So my willingness to trust it depends on whether I can verify the fix. For a small, isolated bug, I can give it more autonomy. For something that changes the training behavior, I’d still want to inspect it carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI coding tool may propose a fix and that the speaker wants to verify it. It does not express that the model might know better than the speaker how to fix the job.
